# Project Deep Dive (Resume Drill)

[← ByteDance](../README.md) · [Every ByteDance question](../../bytedance.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/project-deep-dive-round)

`deep-dive` `verbal` `ai-safety` `llm` `ownership`

---

## Requirements

A typical opening structure for most technical rounds is:

- **5–10 min**: introduce yourself. Not every interviewer will provide their own introduction.
- **15–30 min**: choose one resume project and discuss its design decisions, technology stack, scale, and your individual role in depth.
- Common follow-ups include: `why did you select X instead of Y?`, `which part was most difficult?`, `what would you change in hindsight?`, and `what scale, latency, or cost objective were you working toward?`.

In MLE rounds, the detailed discussion centers specifically on machine-learning work: the models you trained, the evaluation metric, the gains over the baseline, and how you investigated poor performance.

## Notes

- Recent SWE, Growth, and backend screens still devote 15–30 minutes to resume discussion and project ownership before moving to coding or design. Stability, handling online incidents, ownership, and the most difficult project are frequent starting points.
- Interviewers favor projects in which you can clearly show that you made the technical decisions yourself. In MLE interviews, projects focused on training models generally attract more attention than projects centered on building pipelines.
- The question of “why this rather than that” appears regularly, so every design choice listed on your resume needs a defensible alternative.
- In MLE interviews, be ready for the conversation to shift into ML fundamentals: saying “I used dropout” may lead to a five-minute examination of how dropout behaves during inference.
- A commonly reported failure pattern is presenting a polished story while being unable to explain the implementation details. Be prepared to justify every line of every project bullet.
- Bilingual interviews are frequent, and an interviewer may switch to Chinese when your name is Chinese. Prepare your project presentation in both languages.
- Some interviewers revisit the same project in several rounds; repeated teammate patterns make it wise to prepare 2–3 meaningfully different projects so the discussion does not become repetitive.
- Certain loops rely entirely on project deep dives: several rounds may contain neither coding nor behavioral questions, with the decision instead based on communication efficiency, scope, and alignment with the team’s current work.

## Preparation

- Select 2–3 projects, with each one capable of supporting 30 minutes of detailed questioning. Create a one-page summary for each that includes the goal, scale, your contribution, major technical decisions, alternatives considered, metric effect, and regrets.
- For every design decision in your projects, prepare a 30-second response explaining “why this instead of that.”
- Practice presenting each project in both English and Chinese.
- For MLE projects, also prepare for the ML-theory follow-ups you are likely to receive, such as dropout behavior, normalization selection, the reasoning behind the loss function, and the basis for choosing the model.
- Practice guiding the discussion: begin with a precise problem statement, move through the design space, and then explain your choice. Do not wait for the interviewer to pull out each detail individually; volunteer the important points proactively.
